content: The significant progress achieved in malaria control over the past decade has been accompanied by challenges related to insecticide resistance. The World Health Organization (WHO) maintains a global database and an online mapping tool to consolidate data on the susceptibility of Anopheles mosquitoes to insecticides in malaria-endemic countries. Recent data indicate that nearly 90% of these countries have reported resistance to at least one class of insecticide in their mosquito vectors. Resistance to pyrethroids is particularly widespread, detected in 68% of sites with available data. Resistance to organochlorines has been reported in 64% of sites, while resistance to carbamates and organophosphates is less common, detected in 34% and 28% of sites, respectively. Despite the increasing frequency of pyrethroid resistance, there is currently no evidence of operational failure in vector control programs directly attributable to this resistance. However, based on historical experience, operational failures are likely to occur if effective insecticide resistance management (IRM) strategies are not implemented. These strategies should ideally be introduced early to prevent the spread and intensification of resistance. The overarching principles of IRM were outlined in the Global Plan for Insecticide Resistance Management in Malaria Vectors (GPIRM) in 2012. WHO has also provided detailed guidance on monitoring insecticide resistance, interpreting test results, and making informed decisions in its manual for monitoring insecticide resistance in mosquito vectors. When determining whether adjustments to a national malaria strategic plan are necessary, several factors must be considered for the specific locality. These include current and past levels of malaria transmission, the interventions deployed (including their coverage, usage, and duration of efficacy), the insecticide resistance profile of the main vector species (including resistance intensity and mechanisms), and other entomological data such as vector species distribution and abundance. The susceptibility of mosquitoes to insecticides, as well as the species-specific presence, intensity, and mechanisms of resistance, can guide the selection of appropriate insecticidal products. If mosquitoes are found to be resistant to a particular insecticide, products with a different mode of action should be deployed. However, there are reports of differential susceptibility to insecticides within the same class, raising questions about cross-resistance among pyrethroid products. A review of molecular, laboratory, and field data concluded that differences in adult mosquito mortality in pyrethroid resistance assays do not indicate a true or operationally relevant difference in the performance of commonly used pyrethroids (deltamethrin, permethrin, α-cypermethrin, and λ-cyhalothrin). Consequently, switching between pyrethroid insecticides should not be used as a strategy for managing resistance. This finding aligns with WHO’s current and past positions. Given the widespread resistance to pyrethroids, WHO encourages the development and evaluation of nets treated with alternative insecticides. Key technical principles for addressing insecticide resistance include deploying insecticides judiciously to minimize unnecessary selection pressure and maximize disease control impact. National malaria programs (NMPs) should ensure that insecticides are used carefully and with clear epidemiological benefits. Vector control programs should avoid relying on a single class of insecticide over consecutive years and should diversify from pyrethroids whenever possible to preserve their effectiveness. While pyrethroids will continue to be used for insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) in the near term, they should generally not be deployed for indoor residual spraying (IRS) in areas where pyrethroid ITNs are already in use. IRM principles and methods should be integrated into all vector control programs as a core component of program design. NMPs should collaborate with the agricultural sector to coordinate insecticide use, avoiding the use of the same classes of insecticides for both crop protection and public health within the same geographical area. Routine monitoring of insecticide resistance is essential to inform the selection and deployment of insecticides. The additional costs of deploying new vector control tools as part of a comprehensive IRM response should be weighed against their potential long-term public health impact. Formal economic evaluations are encouraged to assess the incremental costs and effectiveness of potential IRM approaches relative to feasible alternatives. Historically, the most common approach to deploying insecticides for malaria vector control has been “sequential use,” where a single insecticide class is used continuously until resistance renders it less effective, after which a switch is made to an insecticide with a different mode of action. In theory, this approach may allow for a return to the original insecticide class if resistance decreases to undetectable levels. The agricultural industry has had some success in managing resistance by using different insecticides over space and time. Similar strategies, such as mixtures, mosaic spraying, rotations, and combined interventions, have been proposed for malaria vector control to prevent or delay resistance spread. Mixtures involve co-formulations of two or more insecticides with different modes of action. Effective deployment requires that resistance to all insecticides in the mixture is rare, ensuring that mosquitoes surviving one insecticide are likely to be killed by the other. Ideally, all insecticides in a mixture should have similar residual life and bioavailability, though this is challenging to achieve, particularly for long-lasting products like insecticidal nets. For IRS, a mixture of a pyrethroid and a neonicotinoid insecticide has been prequalified by WHO. Rotations involve switching between insecticides with different modes of action at pre-set intervals, regardless of resistance frequencies. The theory is that resistance frequencies will decline or stabilize during the period of non-deployment of a specific insecticide. Mosaic spraying involves deploying insecticides with different modes of action in neighboring geographical areas. While rotations are generally considered more practical, there is limited evidence of the success of these strategies in malaria vector control, and no consensus exists on the best IRM approach for specific situations. The success of a particular approach likely depends on mosquito genetics, behavior, population dynamics, and the chemical properties of the insecticides. To achieve optimal impact against malaria, control measures must be tailored to the geographic area and deployed at sufficient coverage. Without an evidence base or sufficient capacity to deploy interventions appropriately, resources may be used suboptimally. Given the heavy reliance on insecticidal interventions, the environmental impacts and resistance development in local vectors are critical considerations in vector control planning. Inappropriate deployment of insecticides in agriculture and public health programs can lead to avoidable environmental contamination and resistance development. IRM practices should be implemented as part of routine operations rather than waiting for resistance to spread or control failure to occur. A pragmatic approach is needed to select appropriate vector control interventions based on the resistance profile of major malaria vectors in the target area. NMPs should develop and implement national plans for monitoring and managing insecticide resistance in accordance with WHO guidelines. These plans should be revisited regularly to incorporate new information and interventions supported by WHO recommendations. Access to effective vector control interventions must be maintained in most countries where malaria control has been effective, including areas with ongoing transmission and those where transmission has been interrupted but some level of receptivity and vulnerability remains. Malaria elimination is defined as the interruption of local transmission of a specific malaria parasite species in a defined area as a result of deliberate interventions. Following elimination, measures to prevent re-establishment of transmission are usually required. Malaria eradication, on the other hand, is the permanent reduction to zero of the worldwide incidence of infection caused by all human malaria parasite species. Residual transmission refers to the persistence of malaria transmission despite high coverage of interventions like ITNs or IRS. This occurs due to a combination of human and vector behaviors, such as outdoor biting by mosquitoes or people not sleeping in protected houses. The sources and risks of residual transmission vary by location and time. Supplementary interventions, such as larviciding and house screening, may be used in addition to ITNs or IRS to further reduce transmission. Standardized methods for quantifying and characterizing residual transmission are needed to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions in addressing this challenge. Improved knowledge of mosquito bionomics and targeted strategies are essential to address residual transmission effectively.
